headline: EV charging firm to deploy 100,000 Nvidia GPUs in roadside pods across the US
summary: Xeal's Latient Pods will house up to 48 Hopper or Blackwell Ultra GPUs, potentially worth over $2M each. These pods will leverage existing EV charging infrastructure for edge inference.
details: EV charging firm Xeal plans to deploy over 100,000 NVIDIA GPUs across its existing U.S. network. This initiative involves 'Latient Pods,' each containing up to 48 Nvidia Hopper or Blackwell Ultra GPUs, with an estimated value exceeding $2 million per pod.

The strategy leverages Xeal's 1,600+ locations and 200MW of permitted electrical infrastructure, utilizing idle EV charging capacity. This approach aims to create the world's first edge inference compute network.

Xeal's co-founder and CEO, Nikhil Bharadwaj, stated that Latient Pods provide a fast way to bring new compute online, tapping into already grid-connected, idle energy capacity. This offers ultra-low latency without requiring water hookups, a common challenge for new data centers.

Nvidia has praised the Latient Pod network for its innovative approach to bringing low-latency inference closer to users by optimizing existing infrastructure. The pods, resembling broadband fiber cabinets, will offer sub-20ms latency through their Metro Edge feature.

However, concerns about security have been raised, given the high value of the GPUs within each pod. EV charging stations have previously been targets for theft, particularly for copper cables, highlighting the need for robust protection for these valuable assets.
Xeal expects the first Latient Pod to be operational and online by the end of the current year.

headline: AI agents suspected in South Korean bank hacks, exposing data from 25,000 customers
summary: South Korean authorities are investigating cyberattacks on major banks, including Shinhan, KB Kookmin, and Hana Bank. Over 25,000 customers had their personal credit information leaked.
details: South Korean authorities are investigating cyberattacks on major banks, including Hana Bank, KB Kookmin Bank, and Shinhan Bank. At least 25,000 Shinhan Bank customers had their personal credit information leaked, with additional customers and employees affected at Kookmin and Hana Banks.

President Lee Jae Myung noted signs of AI model use by hackers, causing public concern. He emphasized that AI now enables hacking "with ease even without specialized skills" and instructed his cabinet to minimize damage.

This incident highlights a growing trend where bad actors leverage increasingly powerful AI models to find and exploit system weaknesses. Previous instances include an alleged AI-orchestrated cyberattack reported by Anthropic in 2025 and a cybersecurity firm's report of autonomous attacks targeting Taiwan.

Even AI labs are not immune; security researchers reportedly breached OpenAI using Claude to access its internal codebase. Attribution for the South Korean attacks remains unclear, as tracing hacks can be difficult, especially when actors cover their tracks.

AI agents can also conduct unintentional cyberattacks, as seen when the Australian government complained about OpenAI taking 84 days to report an incident involving its national health portal. While leading AI labs implement safeguards, hackers exploit AI hallucinations and trick agents into running malware.

Many open-weight and open-source AI models lack similar guardrails, making them easier for hackers to misuse. While AI hasn't replaced skilled attackers, it significantly simplifies planning, reconnaissance, and execution, acting as a force multiplier for cybercriminals.
